title: The Grand Tour
description: The Grand Tour is a syllabus. Primary works appear roughly in the order they were written. Laboratories, exercises, and module chapters are woven through the sequence. Where a work lists passages, those are the intended reading; otherwise, read the whole work. Long mathematical texts are worked alongside other books. Begin at the top and proceed at your own pace.

sections.title: Ancient Greece
sections.description: From Homer to Ptolemy: the founding works of Western literature, philosophy, mathematics, and natural science. The Greek language module runs alongside, offered as an optional companion for those who want to read the originals.

items.note: This book takes time, aim for 3 - 5 propositions a day while reading through the rest of the texts. Finish before starting Ptolemy.
Optional. Begin the Greek language thread here if you want to read alongside the texts.
The grammarians' own account of the language, available as reference from here onward

passages: The Epidemics, Books I and III

items.note: Includes exercises drawn from Plato and Euclid.
Standalone observational lab; no surviving Eratosthenes primary text in the corpus. Precedes the parallax lab, which builds on its method.
Finish Euclid before starting this.

sections.title: Rome & Late Antiquity
sections.description: From Lucretius to Boethius: natural philosophy, engineering, and empire under the Roman peace, ending in the long twilight of the ancient world. The Bible is read in stations across the section, and classical mathematics opens here with Diophantus — met in its own terms, to be taken up by the algebra of the eras ahead.

items.note: The Bible is read in five stations across this section; begin here with the Law.
The Greek thread closes here; the translation exercises point onward for those who continue. The New Testament itself arrives later in the section.

A long-runner, like Euclid before it — two or three problems a day alongside the rest. Read him in his own terms; the supplement shows what his notation actually looked like, and why Heath's page reads as modern algebra.
passages: Book I: the Preliminary; then Problems 1–39

items.note: Read for its philosophy of number, not as a manual — the Pythagorean vision of arithmetic as first among the sciences.
passages: Book II, Chapters 21–29 (28 may be skimmed)

items.note: Nicomachus describes Eratosthenes' sieve at I. 13. Run it, and Euclid's method for the greatest common measure, by hand.
Second station: the histories, wisdom, and the prophets.
Read whole. Herodotus you can sample; Thucydides is one sustained argument — the speeches and the Sicilian catastrophe land because of all that builds to them.
Read as the pair Plutarch built; he compares them in Alexander’s opening lines.

Book V: Introduction and Chapters I, III–V, X
Book VI: Introduction and Chapters I, III, VI–VII

items.note: By now you have lived with the Arithmetica; Archimedes's own epigram rewards its indeterminate methods.
A detour off Arithmetica II.8 — a question worth forming a belief about, and carrying forward.
The atomist account of nature — read against the teleology of the Analytics and the natural histories around it.
Third station: the Gospels, read against the poem you have just finished. If you kept the Greek thread, John's prologue is where it pays.
John's prologue in the original — the first Koine you read for yourself, and the payoff of Chapter 7.
An encyclopedia, not a treatise — the recommendations are doors in. Follow whatever catches you and leave the rest.
Pliny's eight books on plants are not read through. Take him into a garden instead.
The theory of deduction — read the two Analytics together here, alongside the sciences they underwrite.
Read the preface for Hero's account of air and the void; the labs that follow put his devices in your hands.
Seven books; take them one at a time between other readings.

items.note: He is answering what you have already read — Aristotle's nature that does nothing in vain, and the atomism of Lucretius.
The last of the historians you have read in sequence — and the one writing under what Herodotus's Persians only debated.
Fourth station: Luke and Acts are one work in two volumes — the life, then what followed from it.

passages: Book III: the Petitions and the Axioms (optional)
items.note: You have done Euclid; now read a philosopher who thinks the Elements are about being. The prologues are the prize — the commentary proper is there to dip into.
Read for the form as much as the doctrine, and do not linger.

passages: From the Ethical Fragments: Hipparchus, Archytas, and Polus

items.note: Read in his own architecture: the polemic first, then the two cities in origin, in history, and in their ends.
Fifth station: the vision of the end, read as the ancient world itself draws to its close.

sections.title: Islamic Golden Age & Medieval Europe
sections.description: From al-Khwarizmi to Dante: the centuries in which Greek thought was preserved by being argued with, and in which a mathematics owing nothing to Euclid was built out of problems and procedures. Algebra arrives written in sentences, and the numerals arrive with it; by Fibonacci both are moving west. The question of what reason may settle and what it may not is asked here in three traditions at once. The section ends at a threshold rather than a conclusion.

items.note: Read the mathematical chapters only; the rest is astronomy. Zero is handled here as a number with rules of its own, and so are quantities less than nothing. The book al-Khwarizmi wrote beside the Algebra was called On Calculation with Hindu Numerals — this is what he meant.
passages: Chapter 18: Kuttaka (the pulveriser) — the rules for zero and negatives

items.note: Short, and worth reading early: an inheritance being taken stock of rather than received.

The spine of the section. There is not a symbol in it: every equation is a sentence, every solution a procedure, and the proofs at the back are Greek geometry pressed into service. Work the six cases until you can state them without looking.
passages: The six cases and their solutions

items.note: A long-runner — a few sections a week alongside the rest. Watch what he does when an authority and an observation disagree, and how often he builds an apparatus rather than an argument.

items.note: A scholar of one civilisation reading another in its own language, and candid in the preface about what makes the attempt hard. Read that preface before anything else; take the eighty chapters in parts thereafter.

items.note: The Proslogion is a few pages and one argument. Read it twice, and try to say exactly where it would fail before reading anyone who says so.
Read whole and at leisure, alongside the mathematics. The man who wrote these also wrote a treatise solving cubic equations by intersecting conics.
The second spine text, and the point at which the numerals move west. Long — read the opening on the nine figures, then problems as they interest you. Compare his procedures with al-Khwarizmi's.

items.note: Whole, and at whatever pace it takes. The last book in the section written inside the world the section describes.
The threshold. Short, autobiographical, and written in French so that anyone could read it — which is itself the argument. Its own appendix on geometry waits at the start of the next section.
